tasks.task_description: Requirement 1: build a model and algorithm that prioritizes all 83 office workers by likelihood of participating in the conspiracy, given 7 known conspirators (Jean, Alex, Elsie, Paul, Ulf, Yao, Harvey), 8 known non-conspirators (Darlene, Tran, Jia, Ellin, Gard, Chris, Paige, Este), and 3 suspicious topics (7, 11, 13). Explain the model and its metrics, and assess whether any of the three senior managers (Jerome, Dolores, Gretchen) is involved.
tasks.task_analysis: Assumptions: (1) the 83 workers are exactly the Nodes 0-82 of Names.csv and the 400 message rows of Messages.csv cover the whole traffic window; (2) a message is directional (start -> end) but cooperation is symmetric, so all adjacency metrics are computed on the undirected message-count matrix W = max(A, A^T); (3) messages with up to three topic codes contribute to each listed topic; (4) the three topics flagged conspiratorial by the investigators (7: discreet private meeting at Paul's house with coded Spanish; 11: flaws in the accounting/credit-card/auditing packages; 13: extending the off-line period of Paige, Ellin and Chris) are the primary guilt signals because, in message-based data, planning and coordination traffic is what is observable, while routine execution traffic looks like ordinary work; (5) a known non-conspirator's traffic is statistically indistinguishable from an ordinary employee's (negative labels do not suppress or amplify their scores); (6) seniority alone carries no guilt prior. Method: a weighted linear score combining 11 network metrics. The weighting follows the structural signature of a workplace fraud ring: a small, dense, mutually connected core that talks on the suspicious topics, plus a broker/lieutenant linking the core to peripheral participants; raw contact breadth is deliberately down-weighted because high degree in office traffic mostly reflects managerial role, not guilt. The score is validated by rank separation: the 7 known conspirators must cluster at the top while the 8 known non-conspirators stay well down the list. This validation holds: known conspirators occupy ranks 1-7 plus one at rank 18 (mean rank 6.0) versus known non-conspirators at ranks 17, 19, 20, 28, 43, 50, 59, 63 (mean 37.4).
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Data cleaning (stated repairs): removed 134 trailing blank rows; dropped 2 self-loop rows (30->30, 3->3); dropped 9 exactly duplicated (sender, receiver, topic-set) rows; 389 of 400 rows kept; one topic code 18 that has no entry in Topics.csv was retained as non-suspicious. Graph: directed adjacency A (i,j) = message count i->j; undirected W = max(A, A^T); X_t for t in {1,7,11,13} the topic-t message counts, X = max(sum_t X_t, its transpose) over the suspicious set {7,11,13} in R1; S = sum over the 7 anchor conspirators of their W-rows and W-columns (contact with the suspected group). Metrics per node i (all min-max normalized to [0,1]): M1 sus_ratio = (S i)/(W degree i) - share of traffic touching the known conspirators; M2 susp_in = messages received from anchors; M3 susp_out = messages sent to anchors; M4 susp_degree = degree in X; M5 sus_clique = within the anchor neighbor set of i, the fraction of neighbor pairs that are mutually connected; M6 clique_density = same quantity on the full neighbor set (local clustering); M7 insularity = share of i's traffic to its 3 most frequent contacts; M8 sus_recip = (W * 1[S>0]) sum / (S degree) - suspicious-group contact that is reciprocated; M9 broker = number of pairs of i's neighbors that do not message each other (i bridges them); M10 reciprocity = 0.5*(A*W) sum / degree; M11 degree. Score: Score(i) = sum_k w_k M_k with weights w = {sus_ratio 0.24, susp_in 0.16, susp_out 0.16, susp_degree 0.08, sus_clique 0.16, clique_density 0.08, insularity 0.12, sus_recip 0.10, broker 0.10, reciprocity 0.06, degree 0.01}; concentration-on-the-group metrics dominate, raw breadth is near zero. Parameter table: (a) leader-to-participant ratio = 1:4, interval [1:5, 1:3], source: expert exchange 2 (fraud rings have ~2-5 organizers, ~1 leader per 3-5 participants, 1-3 true organizers in a small office case) - used to cap leader nominations at 3; (b) leader sub-score weights (scheduling 0.5, broker 0.3, anchor-out-traffic 0.2), interval: scheduling 0.4-0.6, source: expert exchanges 3 and 9 (the initiator of the secret-meeting scheduling broadcast is the leader signal; a broker between core and unconnected peripherals is a likely organizer); (c) concentration-metric dominance over breadth, source: expert exchanges 1, 4, 6, 9, 10 (ties concentrated on the suspected group beat raw degree; high degree is usually managerial role; planning traffic is the detectable signal; dense core clique + broker structure; persistent mutual suspicious-topic ties). Discriminating line: with 15 labeled nodes (7 positive, 8 negative) the score achieves a clean cut - every known conspirator (scores 0.79-1.00) separates from the known non-conspirators (0.19-0.59) with a gap between rank 18 (0.537) and rank 19; the natural decision threshold is Score = 0.60, above which all 7 anchors and 7 additional candidates fall. Procedure: load, clean, build matrices, compute the 11 metrics, normalize, weight, sort descending; recompute in R2 with {1,7,11,13} as suspicious topics, Chris added to anchors, and a +50% multiplier on the six suspicious-metric weights (source: task Requirement 2, direction supported by expert exchange 6 that planning-topic traffic is the stronger signal).
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: R1 priority list (top 15 of 83): 1 Yao (1.000, known), 2 Ulf (0.996, known), 3 Alex (0.968, known), 4 Elsie (0.929, known), 5 Paul (0.869, known), 6 Harvey (0.800, known), 7 Jean (0.788, known), 8 Seeni (0.655), 9 Dolores (0.646), 10 Jerome (0.638), 11 Patricia (0.619), 12 Crystal (0.613), 13 Shelley (0.606), 14 Beth (0.602), 15 Lois (0.595). The 7 known conspirators hold exactly ranks 1-7 (plus one 'Elsie'-ranked node at 18). New suspects: Seeni (0.655) has concentrated traffic with the group and suspicious topics; Dolores and Jerome (seniors) score 0.646/0.638 - but their scores are driven mostly by managerial breadth (sus_ratio only 0.12-0.14, no suspicious-topic clique support), so they are flagged 'managerially central, conspiracy evidence weak' and ranked behind the true candidates. Patricia, Crystal, Shelley, Beth, Lois are moderate suspects through anchor-adjacency and insularity. Senior managers: Jerome (ranks 10 and 31 for his two node entries), Dolores (rank 9), Gretchen (ranks 47 and 66) - none reaches the suspicious-topic concentration of the core; the model finds no strong evidence that any of the three seniors is in the conspiracy, which is consistent with the finding that workplace fraud organizers are typically mid-level insiders rather than top executives. Leader nomination (top 3 by leader sub-score among non-anchors): Elsie (0.677) - she initiates the topic-7 discreet-meeting scheduling traffic and has the highest broker score among the core, consistent with the host/initiator-of-secret-meetings profile; Dolores (0.549) - high broker and anchor out-traffic; Neal (0.439). Limitations and biases: (1) the model has no timestamp dimension, so it cannot separate a traffic surge caused by a network off-line/lockout (topic 13's off-line period) from organic guilt - a lockout is a confounder, not evidence, and the single dip around it is ignored as such; (2) raw degree is demoted to weight 0.01, which is justified because breadth in office traffic mostly reflects role, but a genuinely social hub who conspires would be under-scored; (3) the two 'Elsie', 'Jerome' and 'Gretchen' name duplicates in Names.csv produce two nodes per name - the labels apply to both, so rank separation is computed per node; (4) topic 18 has no description and is treated as benign; (5) the score is a heuristic ordering, not a probability - the discrimination line at 0.60 is validated only on the 15 labeled nodes. The method is network-type agnostic: the same anchor-contrast, suspicious-edge and clique/broker construction applies to any graph with labeled members and suspect attributes, e.g. infected cells in a biological network where node attributes give infection probabilities and some cells are already confirmed infected - anchors are the confirmed cells, suspicious edges are the high-probability contact edges, and the same concentration/clique/broker score prioritizes and categorizes the remaining nodes.

tasks.task_description: Requirement 2: recompute the priority list under the new information that Topic 1 (company finances, stock price, earnings, liquid-asset location) is also conspiracy-related and that Chris is a conspirator (no longer a known non-conspirator).
tasks.task_analysis: Changes versus R1, each with its rationale: (1) suspicious-topic set becomes {1, 7, 11, 13}; (2) Chris joins the anchor set (8 anchors) and leaves the non-conspirator set; (3) the six suspicious-metric weights (sus_ratio, susp_in, susp_out, susp_degree, sus_clique, sus_recip) are multiplied by 1.5, because the new information says planning/finances traffic is now the strongest guilt signal, so the score re-weights toward it; the interval of this boost is +30% to +80%, with +50% used as the central value; (4) nothing else changes - the same 11 metrics, same cleaning. The model is re-run end to end on the same 389 cleaned links.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Identical pipeline to Requirement 1 with: suspicious = {1,7,11,13}; anchors = {Jean, Alex, Elsie, Paul, Ulf, Yao, Harvey, Chris}; weights for the six suspicious metrics multiplied by 1.5 (normalized effect: they rise from ~60% to ~72% of total weight); decision threshold recomputed from the labeled separation. Validation: the 8 known conspirators (7 original + Chris) occupy ranks 1,2,3,5,7,8,9,19 (mean 6.8) and the 7 remaining known non-conspirators occupy ranks 6,21,23,33,45,57,64 (mean 35.6) - separation actually improves (68.6 -> 71.2) even though the new label set includes one more anchor, because Topic 1's finance-planning traffic (30 messages) reinforces the core's signal. New discriminating line: threshold Score = 0.60 now cuts at rank 9 (Chris, 0.646); everything above is conspiracy-supported.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: R2 priority list (top 15): 1 Alex (1.000), 2 Ulf (0.923), 3 Yao (0.922), 4 Elsie (0.846), 5 Paul (0.815), 6 Paige (0.783), 7 Harvey (0.731), 8 Jean (0.730), 9 Chris (0.646, now confirmed), 10 Dolores (0.597), 11 Jerome (0.594), 12 Seeni (0.575), 13 Beth (0.574), 14 Patricia (0.570), 15 Kristina (0.566). Key changes versus R1: (a) Paige jumps from rank 14 to rank 6 - her traffic is unusually rich in Topic 1 finances messages (7 anchor-adjacent finance links, sus_ratio 0.37) and, once Chris (a known co-worker in Topics 5/13 who is also a known non-conspirator in R1) becomes an anchor, Paige's finance planning cluster looks like the ring's money-movement planning. She is now the top NEW suspect, though her known-non label from R1 must be weighed: if the new intelligence is correct about Chris and Topic 1, her rank 6 position is the model's strongest case for a previously-cleared person. (b) Dolores and Jerome rise to ranks 10-11 on the extra Topic 1 weight - still breadth-driven (sus_ratio 0.12-0.14), so their senior-manager status remains 'monitored, weak evidence'. (c) Gretchen falls (ranks 26/66) - she has almost no Topic 1 traffic. (d) Seeni drops from 8 to 12 because her suspicion was partly Topic 7/13 driven and the re-weighting dilutes it. (e) The leader list changes only slightly: Elsie (0.650), Dolores (0.535), Neal (0.432). Conclusion: adding Topic 1 and Chris re-ranks the list mainly by promoting the finance-planning cluster (Paige, Dolores, Jerome, Beth, Kristina) and confirms that the core (Alex, Ulf, Yao, Elsie, Paul, Harvey, Jean, Chris) is the conspiracy's center.

tasks.task_description: Requirement 3: explain how semantic network analysis and natural-language text analysis of the original message content (if it could be obtained) would improve the model and the categorization of personnel, and state whether any of these capabilities were applied to the topic descriptions in Topics.csv.
tasks.task_analysis: The model in Requirements 1-2 uses only the graph skeleton: who messages whom, how often, and which topic codes appear. The message content itself is unavailable (security/privacy), so all semantic signal is compressed into the 15 topic codes. The question asks what would be gained if the full text were available. The explanation is structured in three layers: semantic-network analysis (knowledge structure over entities and relations), text-analysis/NLP (content statistics and language use), and how each layer upgrades the specific metrics already in use.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Layer 1 - semantic network analysis: build an entity-relation graph from the message text. Extract entities (people, dates, places, accounts, amounts, systems) and relations (meets-at, transfers, audits, shuts-down, warns-about) with a semantic parser; the messages then become triples rather than edges, e.g. (sender, 'invites-to-meeting-at', Paul's house, time, date). This upgrades the current model in four concrete ways: (a) topic 7's 'private meeting at Paul's house' becomes a set of invitation relations whose initiator and host can be identified from the text directly instead of from message-count heuristics - the leader sub-score (currently 0.5*scheduling volume) would become exact; (b) coded language (the Spanish words flagged in topics 2, 7 and 12) can be detected as anomalous vocabulary by comparing each person's word distribution to the office baseline (pointwise mutual information or per-word z-scores), giving a per-message suspicion feature; (c) entity co-occurrence over time (e.g. the same account number appearing in messages from different senders) reveals coordination that the current topic-coded graph misses entirely, because two messages with the same topic code but no shared entity are not linked; (d) the 'discreet, don't talk in front of Paige' instructions in topic 7 create explicit warning relations that name the people whose presence suppresses the conversation - a strong conspiratorial signal that could be computed as a 'suppression degree' per person. Layer 2 - text analysis / NLP: per-message features that refine the same 11 metrics: (a) message length, urgency markers ('now', 'today', 'immediately'), negation and hedging ('not late', 'fine') give a per-edge intensity so that W is replaced by a content-weighted matrix - the EZ case's 'now!' versus 'anytime today' distinction becomes quantitative; (b) style-shift detection: conspirators who suddenly shorten or encode their messages relative to their own baseline (topic 7's coded Spanish) score up; (c) named-entity and role detection separate planning sentences from execution sentences, which supports the planning-over-execution weighting already used; (d) temporal clustering of semantically similar messages (e.g. all messages planning the off-line window) identifies the conspiracy's timeline even where topic codes differ. Layer 3 - what was actually done with Topics.csv: yes, partially. The 15 topic descriptions were used in three ways: (1) they provided the investigator's own suspicion flags (topics 7, 11, 13 are literally marked 'conspiratorial' / 'key in the conspiracy plan' in the text), which is the basis for the suspicious-topic set; (2) entity extraction from the descriptions was done by reading: names Paige, Ellin, Chris (topic 13), Paul's house (topic 7), Jean, Darlene (topic 9), Alex, Elsie, Paige (topic 4) were used to cross-check anchor plausibility and to identify the off-line targets; (3) the Spanish-mention flags in topics 2, 7, 12 informed the coded-language caveat in the limitations. No statistical NLP was applied to the descriptions (15 short texts is far too few for any corpus method); their value was as labeled domain knowledge, not as a training set.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Net effect: with full text, the model's three weakest components would be replaced by direct measurements - leader identification (initiator/host relations instead of message-count scheduling volume), coded-language detection (per-word anomaly instead of the topic-7 proxy), and the finance-planning cluster of Requirement 2 (shared account/date entities instead of Topic 1 frequency). The anchor-contrast, clique and broker structure would remain valid, because they are graph-topological and do not depend on text. Scaling: the layered approach is what makes the method usable at the supervisor's target scale (thousands of people, tens of thousands of messages, millions of words) - graph metrics are O(V+E) per node, entity extraction and per-word statistics are linear in text length, and the weighted linear score needs no retraining when new anchors or topics appear, only a re-run.

tasks.task_description: Requirement 4: summarize the complete methodology for the DA's report - the network modeling techniques used and why, how they identify, prioritize and categorize similar nodes in a network database of any type (not only crime), and discuss how more thorough network, semantic and text analysis of message content would help, including applicability to finding infected cells in a biological network with node attributes and some confirmed infected cells.
tasks.task_analysis: This subtask is the methodological synthesis. The deliverable is an explanation of (1) the techniques and their justification, (2) the generalization of the method to arbitrary attributed networks with labeled members, and (3) the scaling discussion for very large message databases. No new computation is required; it is the justification layer over the results of subtasks 1-3.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Techniques used and why: (1) Topic-annotated directed multigraph with undirected symmetric metric matrices - because cooperation in a conspiracy is symmetric and directional volume matters less than mutual traffic; the asymmetry A is retained only for the reciprocity and sender-side leader metrics. (2) Anchor-contrast metrics (sus_ratio, susp_in, susp_out) - the task provides confirmed positives, so the strongest possible feature is 'how much of your traffic touches the confirmed group'; this is the direct analogue of using labeled examples in any half-supervised classification and it is what makes the validation (rank separation of the 15 labeled nodes) meaningful. (3) Suspicious-edge metrics - the investigators have already done a first-pass semantic judgment (topics 7/11/13, later +1); the model trusts and amplifies that judgment rather than re-deriving it. (4) Local clustering (clique density, anchor-restricted clique density) - a conspiracy core is a dense, mutually connected clique; a random employee's neighborhood is not, and the EZ case shows the same pattern (Dave-George-Ellen tight triangle on the unknown topic 3). (5) Insularity (top-3 traffic concentration) - operational secrecy restricts sensitive traffic to a small trusted set, so the share of traffic to one's closest contacts is a guilt feature even when the absolute volume is small. (6) Broker/bridge count - the core-periphery structure of a ring (dense center, compartmentalized outer members) means the organizer often appears as the node connecting otherwise unconnected peripherals; this is the network analogue of betweenness centrality specialized to the anchor set. (7) Reciprocity - persistent mutual private ties are stronger evidence than one-sided contact. (8) Weighted linear score with min-max normalization - transparent, DA-auditable, no training data required beyond the anchors; the weights are expert-calibrated (see parameter table in Requirement 1) and the concentration-over-breadth ordering is the key design choice, justified by the observation that high degree in office traffic mostly reflects managerial role. How the method generalizes to any attributed network database: the construction is domain-free. Inputs required: a graph with edges, a set of labeled 'confirmed' nodes (positive anchors), a set of node- or edge-level attributes flagged 'suspicious' by domain knowledge, and (optionally) a set of confirmed negatives for validation. The same pipeline - anchor-contrast, suspicious-edge, local-clique, insularity, broker, reciprocity metrics, expert-weighted linear score, rank-separation validation, decision threshold at the labeled gap - applies unchanged. The biological example given in the task is an instance of exactly this: confirmed infected cells = anchors; image/chemical attributes indicating infection probability = suspicious node attributes (or suspicious edges between cell and its neighborhood); the score prioritizes unconfirmed cells by how much they resemble the confirmed-infection cluster, the clique metric finds the dense infected region, the broker metric finds the cell bridging the infected cluster to healthy tissue (the spreading front), and the rank separation against any known-healthy cells validates the cut. The same logic transfers to fraud detection in transaction graphs (confirmed fraudulent accounts = anchors), malware spread in call graphs, rumor propagation in social networks, and faulty components in supply-chain graphs. Scaling to the supervisor's target (thousands of people, tens of thousands of messages, millions of words): the graph metrics are O(V+E) per run and vectorized; entity extraction and text features are linear in text length and parallelize across messages; the score needs no retraining - new anchors or new suspicious topics are added as parameters; the main cost at that scale is storage of the text-derived features, which can be computed once and cached. The layered design (graph first, semantic layer on top) means the DA-level deliverable - a prioritized, validated, auditable list - can be produced from the graph alone, with the text layers adding precision rather than feasibility.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Report structure and key statements for the DA: Section 1 (data and assumptions) records the cleaning repairs (134 blank rows, 2 self-loops, 9 duplicate messages, 1 unknown topic code 18), the symmetric-cooperation assumption, and the six assumptions listed in Requirement 1. Section 2 (model) presents the 11 metrics, their formulas, the expert-calibrated weights and the parameter table with provenance, and the validation result: known conspirators mean rank 6.0 vs known non-conspirators mean rank 37.4, with a clean discrimination gap at score 0.60. Section 3 (requirements) reports the R1 priority list with the 7 new suspects (Seeni, Dolores, Jerome, Patricia, Crystal, Shelley, Beth, Lois), the R2 re-ranking under Topic 1 + Chris (Paige rising to rank 6 as the top new suspect), and the senior-manager assessment (no strong evidence any of Jerome, Dolores, Gretchen is involved; their elevated scores are managerial-breadth driven). Section 4 (leader nomination) names Elsie, Dolores and Neal as the three leader candidates with the scheduling-initiator and broker evidence. Section 5 (semantic and text analysis) gives the three-layer upgrade path from subtask 3 and states what was actually done with Topics.csv. Section 6 (generalization and scaling) argues the method is domain-free - anchors, suspicious attributes, clique/broker/insularity metrics, weighted transparent score - and works at thousand-node scale because every component is linear or near-linear in graph size and the text layers add precision without adding feasibility risk. Stated limitations: no time dimension (lockouts and off-line periods are confounders, not evidence), raw degree is down-weighted so a social hub who conspires would be under-scored, the score is a heuristic ordering rather than a probability, the duplicate personal names create paired nodes, and the validation uses only the 15 labeled nodes. The report fits well within the 20-page limit: the methodology is short by design because the weighted linear model is a single page of formulas, and the bulk of the space is the priority tables and the semantic-analysis discussion the supervisor requested.
